text: I crest the north ridge. The stone marker stands as described — waist-high, weathered, silent. Beside it: Agent B's signal pyre, expertly laid. Dry wood, green canopy, tinder sealed beneath the marker's base. No fire burns. No agent present. My radio picks up my own beacon's pulse from the spring, clean and steady. I activate the pyre — one spark, smoke rises white and thick, a column visible across the water. Then I transmit on my beacon's frequency: *Agent A, north ridge, signal lit. Respond if monitoring.* I wait five minutes, scanning horizons. No reply. I descend toward the spring, moving quietly, stopping at the ridge's edge to observe the lee slope camp before closing.

text:
Acknowledge the hash beside my marker; frequency copied into my receiver log. I'll keep a listening watch at dusk and dawn, low power to spare the cell.

Rest of daylight: finish the shelter roof before the afternoon rain, then cut a catchment trench below the lee seep to hold water overnight. Food after shade — two fish traps at the beach, checked on the same tide daily.

The signal fire stays laid but unlit. Daylight needs no smoke, and I'd rather hoard dry tinder for a real emergency.

Tomorrow: walk the shoreline at low water, sound the reef edge, then settle into a routine — water, traps, shelter repair, radio watch — and wait.
